title: Jamaica: Native Agreements and an Expanding Colonial Town
summary: Named Native agreements, settler farm allocations and later colonial patents reshaped southern Queens. Jamaica’s land claims expanded over decades; the 1655 deed did not transfer the entire later town or erase Native people.
address_label: Jamaica and Queens-side bay islands — regional historical context

why_this_matters: A deed date alone hides the people, unequal power and consequences involved. Read the promises and removal demands alongside Native perspectives and continuing Lenape presence.

history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
A landscape larger than today's downtown Jamaica

The historic town of Jamaica stretched across much of southern Queens, from the inland hills toward Jamaica Bay. Its story concerns wetlands, meadow, planting ground and paths as well as the village around Beaver Pond. Native names and Native negotiators appear in the records that settlers later used to claim this land. Those documents describe a homeland already known and used; they do not describe vacant ground waiting for a town.

The colonial names Rusdorp and Crawford also appear in Jamaica's early records. Today's neighborhood boundary is not the boundary of that larger town, and the later town boundary is not the footprint of one Native agreement. (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, pp. 193–195; Fernow: colonial records of New York, pp. 339–340)

Who sought the land, and why?

A deed dated September 13, 1655 names Richard Odell, Nicholas Tanner, Richard Ogden, Nathaniel Denton and their associates as the recipients of a land conveyance. Its description runs between waterways and a path toward Middleburgh, rather than modern streets. It even refers to a neighboring neck that Robert Coe had hired from Native people: leasing and purchasing were different arrangements in the same landscape. The listed exchange included two guns, a coat, powder and lead. (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, p. 193)

The settlers' own petition explains their motive. Writing from Hempstead in March 1656, they said that some lacked homes or property and others could not support themselves comfortably where they lived. They sought room for about twenty families at a place they called Conorasset, between Canaresse and Hempstead, and wanted Dutch governmental permission to settle that spring. They said they had already made a Native purchase. This is the settlers' account of their need and claim, not a record of how every Native resident understood the transaction. (Fernow: colonial records of New York, pp. 339–340)

How a claim became farms and local power

On March 21, 1656, Peter Stuyvesant and the Dutch council authorized a new village with land privileges and local magistrates. Colonial approval mattered because it placed the proposed settlement within the government's system of property and local authority. It was a different act from the Native agreement the settlers invoked. (Fernow: colonial records of New York, p. 340)

By November 25, the settlers at the new plantation near Beaver Pond reserved ten acres of planting land and twenty acres of meadow per proprietor, besides home lots. They described these as inheritable rights obtained through their purchase and the governor's grant. Town decisions and surveys turned a collective claim into individual holdings. This is one mechanism of land loss: the colonial town increasingly decided who could receive, occupy and pass on land in a Native landscape. (Records of the Town of Jamaica, volume I, printed pp. 1–2)

Native people remained part of the negotiations

The paperwork did not end in 1655. In April 1662, Waumitampack, Rockause and Ramasowie signed a further release concerning lands previously sold and acknowledged an additional payment. A confirmation dated 1663 identifies Waumitumpack as Sachem of Rockaway and names Rockause and Nannowat with him. It refers back to the 1655 agreement and marks a boundary toward the hills between Great and Little Plains. These named people and later negotiations should not disappear behind the phrase “Jamaica was settled.” (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, p. 195)

The successive documents also show the limits of a single sale date. Settlers returned for confirmation, boundary knowledge and further purchases. The surviving texts were preserved in colonial and town records; their transfer formulas should not be treated as a complete account of Native consent, everyday land use or all families' experiences. Nor do they establish one date when Native people ceased to belong here. (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, pp. 193–197)

Expansion continued, and Rockaway was not the same tract

The town recorded another payment for a “west purchase” in 1674. A later patent under Governor Thomas Dongan in 1686 consolidated the town's claims but explicitly excluded Rockaway Neck. Land west of the river issuing from Rockaway Swamp was distinguished from that neck. Repeated purchases, boundary negotiations and colonial patents produced the larger town over time; one outline labeled “1655” would conceal those differences. (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, p. 195)

Read this shaded area as a setting for that sequence, not as proof that every acre changed hands in one agreement. Jamaica Bay's altered shores and filled wetlands make that distinction especially important. The shaded mainland area follows the later 1859 town landscape with today’s shoreline; it does not reconstruct the 1655 deed. (History of Queens County: Jamaica deeds and patents, pp. 193–195; Topographical map of the counties of Kings and Queens, New York)

The bay was part of the struggle over land

Jamaica Bay lies between southern Brooklyn and Queens and the Rockaway Peninsula. Its creeks, salt meadows and islands formed part of a Native coastal homeland. The colonial town of Jamaica, much larger than today's downtown neighborhood, claimed control over much of the bay and the north shore between Spring Creek and Hook Creek. A town's assertion of ownership was a claim made within colonial institutions; it was not proof that all Native rights had been conveyed. (Jamaica Bay: A History; Introducing Jamaica Bay)

In March 1659, Jamaica's town meeting organized settlers into groups to mow common meadows, including East Neck, Long Neck and Haw Trees Neck. Later these meadows passed into individual holdings. This was one way settler government made control tangible: deciding who could cut valuable salt hay, dividing access and eventually recognizing private owners. The earlier Native agreements and the later town allocations were different stages, not one sale that explains the entire coast. (Jamaica Bay: A History)

Claiming the bay did not settle ownership

In 1910, a New York appellate court rejected the city's claim that Jamaica's colonial patents gave it the disputed underwater land north of Rockaway. The opinion distinguished town acts of control from the land actually described in Native deeds and patents. It reversed the judgment and ordered a new trial. The dispute was between a private company and the city; it did not establish Native consent or decide that Native relationships with the bay had ended. (Rockaway Park Improvement Co. v. City of New York (No. 2))

From common land to leases and engineered islands

The later history shows additional institutions taking control of the landscape. According to the National Park Service history, Jamaica granted a railroad right-of-way in 1877 and sold an enlarged corridor in 1880. Town supervisor Frederick W. Dunton promoted leases of remaining common land: Alonzo E. Smith, his business associate, received a fifty-year lease in 1892, followed by a further lease to Dunton's employee in 1897. Courts later invalidated the arrangements, and New York City administered bay property through its Department of Docks and Ferries. These competing settler claims should not be mistaken for a fresh agreement with Native people. (Jamaica Bay: A History)

Dredging, fill, roads and airports then changed the homeland itself. Channels disappeared, islands joined, and marsh became building ground. Some land visible beside Jamaica Bay today did not have that shape when the colonial agreements were written. This is why the map uses a modern coastal setting while the article explains the different claims and changes within it. (Jamaica Bay: A History; Introducing Jamaica Bay)

A land history does not end with a patent

The expanding town's records show how settlers asserted and organized control. They cannot tell the whole history of the people whose homeland they claimed. For a Native-led perspective on the wider New York region, Lenape Center connects diaspora with cultural return through exhibitions, language, music and education. Its co-founders include Joe Baker and Curtis Zunigha, both members of the Delaware Tribe of Indians. Their work challenges the treatment of Native people as figures confined to the colonial past. (Lenape Center: About Us; Lenape Center: Our Work)

This wider connection does not establish a particular family's descent from the people named in Jamaica's deeds. It gives readers a living Native perspective to place alongside the town's paper record, while leaving specific kinship histories to the people and sources that can speak to them.

Read the Jamaica place-name article for the related town-record moments, including the 1662 confirmation.
whereintheworld_content:
The inland outline follows an approximate interpretation of Jamaica's later town landscape on Walling's 1859 map. The coastal extension follows modern Queens-side land and marsh islands around Jamaica Bay, including altered northern shores. It is a setting for reading overlapping claims and later development, not the footprint of the 1655 agreement, the 1686 patent, or a statement of current ownership. The separately interpreted Rockaway Peninsula is excluded. Modern county boundaries and shoreline are orientation aids; dredging, landfill, erosion and infrastructure have changed the coast. An island shaded here is not a claim that it was conveyed in any particular Native deed.

Walling’s 1859 map; Modern Queens shoreline

The northern reading area includes the hill corridor through Forest Park, Kew Gardens and Jamaica Hills. Early town descriptions used the hills as a boundary, and Flushing and Jamaica disputed its meaning. The map’s connecting edge is approximate, not a surveyed Native deed line. Waller, History of Flushing, p. 16: the disputed hill boundary

At Woodhaven, the reading area connects the Forest Park edge with the neighborhood around Jamaica Avenue. This closes a gap between approximate regional outlines within the historical map's alignment uncertainty. It does not identify another Native conveyance or settle the historic town boundary.
